paragraphs.title: The Psalm’s Heading and God’s Greatness

easy.explanation: The heading identifies it as a psalm of David.
easy.q: To whom is the psalm attributed in its heading?
What instrument is named in the heading?

easy.explanation: The psalm declares, “O LORD our Lord, how excellent is thy name in all the earth!”

answers: The heading identifies the psalm, and the verse begins with praise
The heading describes a battle, and the verse describes a journey
The heading concerns humanity, and the verse concerns only music
medium.explanation: The heading identifies the psalm, which immediately begins by praising the LORD.
medium.q: How does the opening verse relate to the psalm’s heading?

medium.explanation: In this context, “glory” means God’s majesty and splendor.
medium.q: What does “glory” refer to in “who hast set thy glory above the heavens”?

medium.explanation: The verse speaks of God’s excellent name in the earth and His glory above the heavens.
medium.q: Which two realms are mentioned in the opening declaration?

answers: It moves from the heading and performance setting to universal praise
It moves from the heavens to a list of animals
It moves from human weakness to a military command
challenge.explanation: The psalm moves from its heading to a declaration of God’s greatness throughout creation.
challenge.q: What movement of thought occurs at the beginning of the psalm?

answers: God’s greatness is limited to one place
God is present only in the heavens
challenge.explanation: Together, the earth and heavens present a universal picture of God’s greatness.
challenge.q: What is suggested by mentioning both the earth and the heavens?

challenge.explanation: “Excellent” expresses the greatness and splendor of God’s name.
challenge.q: Which word most clearly emphasizes the excellence of God’s name?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings hast thou ordained strength.”
easy.q: From whose mouth has strength been ordained?

easy.explanation: The verse refers to “thine enemies,” as well as “the enemy and the avenger.”
easy.q: Against whom is this strength connected?

answers: It stills the enemy and the avenger
easy.explanation: The stated purpose is “that thou mightest still the enemy and the avenger.”
easy.q: What does the ordained strength accomplish?

answers: It becomes a means by which the enemy is silenced
It causes the children to leave the land
It describes the animals of the field
medium.explanation: The verse connects strength from children’s mouths with stilling the enemy and avenger.
medium.q: How is the praise of children connected with opposition to enemies?

medium.explanation: “Babes and sucklings” refers to infants and very young children.
medium.q: In this passage, what does “babes and sucklings” describe?

medium.explanation: Here, “still” means to silence or quiet the enemy.
medium.q: What does “still” mean in “that thou mightest still the enemy”?

answers: It comes from children rather than warriors
It comes from the stars rather than the earth
It comes from animals rather than people
challenge.explanation: The verse presents babes and sucklings as the source through which strength is ordained.
challenge.q: What is surprising about the source of strength in this verse?

answers: The weakness associated with children is used against powerful enemies
The heavens are contrasted with the sea
The animals are contrasted with the stars
challenge.explanation: The verse presents the mouths of the very young as a means of confronting enemies.
challenge.q: What contrast is suggested by the verse?

answers: The ordained strength results in the enemy being silenced
The strength causes the enemy to grow louder
The strength refers only to physical labor
challenge.explanation: The strength ordained from children’s mouths serves to still the enemy and avenger.
challenge.q: How are “strength” and “stilleth” related in the verse’s meaning?

paragraphs.title: Wonder at Creation and the Question of Humanity

easy.explanation: The psalmist considers the heavens, the work of God’s fingers, the moon, and the stars.
The vastness of creation leads the psalmist to wonder and praise.
easy.q: What does the psalmist marvel at?

easy.explanation: The question concerns man and the son of man.
easy.q: About whom does the psalmist ask, “What is man”?

answers: The vastness of creation makes humanity seem small
The heavens are described as weaker than humanity
The heavens are identified as an enemy
medium.explanation: The greatness of the heavens makes the psalmist wonder why God is mindful of human beings.
medium.q: Why does looking at the heavens lead to a question about humanity?

answers: Remembering or giving thoughtful attention to him
medium.explanation: “Mindful” means remembering or giving attention to someone.
medium.q: What does “mindful” mean in “that thou art mindful of him”?

answers: The vastness of creation and the smallness of humanity
medium.explanation: The psalm contrasts the immense heavens with the human being whom God remembers.
medium.q: What contrast appears in these verses?

answers: Why does God remember and visit humanity?
Why were the stars placed in the sea?
challenge.explanation: The question “What is man, that thou art mindful of him?” asks why God gives attention to humanity.
challenge.q: What central question arises from the psalmist’s observation?

answers: It turns the sight of creation into reflection on human significance
It denies the importance of humanity
It changes the heavens into animals
challenge.explanation: The psalmist moves from contemplating creation to considering humanity’s place before God.
challenge.q: What does the movement from observation to questioning accomplish?

answers: Human smallness does not prevent God from caring for humanity
Human beings matter only because they are physically large
Humanity has no place in creation
challenge.explanation: The verses hold together human smallness and God’s mindful attention.
challenge.q: What is implied by humanity being small yet remembered by God?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “thou hast crowned him with glory and honour.”
easy.q: With what has God crowned humanity?

easy.explanation: Humanity is given dominion over “the works of thy hands.”
easy.q: Over what has humanity been given dominion?

answers: Sheep, oxen, beasts, birds, and fish
easy.explanation: The passage names sheep and oxen, beasts of the field, birds of the air, and fish of the sea.
easy.q: Which group of creatures is listed in these verses?

answers: Humanity is small before the universe but receives honor and authority
Humanity is greater than the heavens and needs no honor
Humanity is unrelated to the rest of creation
medium.explanation: Though small in comparison with creation, humanity is crowned with glory and given dominion.
medium.q: How do human smallness and human dignity fit together?

medium.explanation: “Dominion” means authority or rule over the works of God’s hands.
medium.q: What does “dominion” mean in this passage?

answers: Domestic animals and wild beasts, then birds and sea creatures
medium.explanation: The list moves from sheep and oxen to beasts of the field, birds of the air, and fish of the sea.
medium.q: What is the general order of the creatures named?

answers: It is a gift from God that should be exercised with recognition and responsibility
It is permission to conquer without limits
It proves that humanity is separate from creation
challenge.explanation: The dominion comes from God’s hands and should be understood as a received responsibility.
challenge.q: What value or responsibility is suggested by human dominion?

challenge.explanation: The passage lists animals of the land, air, and sea, but not the stars.
challenge.q: Which part of creation is not included in the animal list?

answers: Dominion is given over “the works of thy hands”
Humanity is said to have created the animals
God is not mentioned in the passage
challenge.explanation: The authority is granted within God’s own works, showing that it comes from Him.
challenge.q: What shows that human authority is not independent of God?

easy.explanation: The final verse repeats the opening declaration of praise.

easy.q: What does the final verse call the LORD?

easy.explanation: The final verse repeats that God’s name is excellent “in all the earth.”
easy.q: Where is the LORD’s name excellent?

answers: The ending repeats the declaration made at the beginning
The ending introduces an entirely unrelated subject
medium.explanation: The psalm begins and ends with the declaration, “O LORD our Lord, how excellent is thy name in all the earth!”
medium.q: What is the relationship between the opening and ending of the psalm?

medium.explanation: “Excellent” expresses greatness and worthiness of praise.
medium.q: What does “excellent” mean in the repeated declaration?

answers: God’s greatness extends throughout the earth
The psalm is mainly about an instrument
Humanity is the only subject of the psalm
medium.explanation: Repeating the line emphasizes the universal excellence of God’s name.
medium.q: What idea is strengthened by the repeated ending?

answers: It closes the psalm with the same central idea with which it began
It removes the importance of creation
challenge.explanation: The repetition creates a frame around the psalm and returns to its central praise.
challenge.q: What is the literary purpose of repeating the declaration at the end?

answers: It connects the themes of humanity and creation to praise of God
It rejects the discussion of humanity and creation
It focuses only on the instrument named in the heading
challenge.explanation: After considering creation and humanity, the psalm returns to praise of the LORD.
challenge.q: How does the ending relate to the middle of the psalm?

challenge.explanation: The word “our” in “O LORD our Lord” expresses the worshipers’ relationship to the LORD.
challenge.q: Which word expresses the relationship between the LORD and the worshipers?
